REFERENCE BY THE CHAIR 
Killing of an employee of Border Roads Organisation in Afghanistan 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, this House expresses its deep shock and 
profound grief over the killing of Shri Maniyappan Raman Kutty, an employee 
of the Border Roads Organisation, who was working on the important Zaranj-
Delaram Road Project in Afghanistan under the aegis of India-Afghan Friendship 
Project on the 23rd November, 2005. The House strongly condemns this cruel 
and barbaric act and hopes that the perpetrators of this heinous crime would be 
brought to justice at the earliest. 
We express our heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family members 
of Shri Kutty.

*43. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Government of Maharashtra has sought the 
relaxation of Coastal Zonal Regulation, 1991 for some areas in Mumbai; 
(b) if so, the names of such areas; 
(c) the reaction of the Central Government thereto; and 
(d) the reasons for not accepting the proposal? 
4 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. For undertaking developmental activities in several areas of 
Greater Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, the State Government of Maharashtra has 
been seeking relaxations of the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification, 
1991 and Coastal Zone Management Plan of Maharashtra from time to time. 
These include: 
(i) Construction of Western Freeway Sea Link from Worli-Bandra to 
Nariman. 
(ii) Development of five housing schemes by Maharashtra Housing and 
Development Authority (MHADA) at Charkop-Kandivli Part-IV, 
Versova Survey No. 120, Andheri (West, Phase-I), Malwani-Malad 
(West), Survey No.263, Gorai (Phase-Ill), Mulund (East) Survey 
No.386 (Phase-I). 
(iii) Construction of Trans Harbour Sea Link from Sewree to Nhava 
Sheva. 
(iv) Increase in Floor Space Index (FSI) for undertaking the project 
pertaining to Rehabilitation of slums and dilapidated structures in 
several areas of Mumbai. 
(v) Development of open spaces in Mumbai. 
(vi) Development of missing link roads. 
(vii) Dumping of municipal solid waste in Coastal Regulation Zone area. 
(viii) Reduction of buffer zone along mangroves. 
(ix) Permitting agriculture in Kharland area falling in inter-tidal areas. 
(c) and (d) No relaxations have been given. However, necessary statutory 
clearances/approvals have been given, under the provisions of Coastal 
Regulation Zone Notification, 1991 and its subsequent amendments in 
respect of all proposals except for SI. Nos. (iv), (vi) and (vii) above. These could 
not be agreed to as the proposed activities are not permissible under the existing 
provisions of Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 1991.

Encouraging investment in agricultural marketing infrastructure 
projects 
 *44. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA:       
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to come out with an innovative scheme 
to encourage entrepreneurs investing in agricultural marketing infrastructure 
projects; 
(b) if so, whether this move is aimed at bringing down risk threat for both 
entrepreneurs and banks; 
(c) whether venture capital scheme was part of Government's effort to bridge 
the gap between producer and consumer; 
(d) whether the scheme covers a wide range of agricultural and allied sectors' 
activities including collection, cleaning, grading, quality, certification, 
labeling, packing, ripening chambers, retailing, wholesale and value addition 
facilities; and 
(e) if so, by when these schemes are likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (e) 
Ministry of Agriculture is implementing a Central Sector Scheme for 
"Development/Strengthening of Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure, 
Grading and Standardization". Under th e scheme, investment subsidy is 
provided @25% on the capital cost of the marketing infrastructure 
development project subject to a maximum of Rs.50 lakh for each project in all 
States and @33.3% of capital cost subject to a maximum of Rs.60 lakh for each 
project in case of North Eastern St ates, hilly areas and to Scheduled 
Castes/Scheduled Tribes entrepreneurs. In respect of infrastructure projects of 
State Governments/State Agencies, there is no upper ceiling on subsidy to be 
provided under the scheme. The Scheme is reform linked, to be implemented 
in those States/Union Territories wherein the law dealing with agricultural 
markets (Agricultural Produce Marketing Regulation Act) allows setting up of 
competitive agricultural markets in private and c ooperative sectors, direct 
marketing and contract farming. The States of Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, 
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Manipur, Sikkim, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, 
Nagaland and 
6 

(25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Union Territory of Andaman & Nicobar Islands have so far been notified to receive 
assistance under the Scheme. 
The Ministry of Agriculture is also implementing a Central Sector Scheme for 
Agri-Business Development by providing venture capital assistance to agri-business 
projects and assisting producers' group in the preparation of detailed reports for such 
projects. The main objective of the Scheme is to catalyze private investment in setting 
up of agribusiness projects and thereby providing assured markets to producers for 
increasing rural income and employment. The scheme has been approved with an 
outlay of Rs.48 crores during remaining period of Tenth Plan. Venture capital 
assistance is provided to eligible projects in the form of equity upto an extent of 26% of 
the project equity or 10% of the total project cost or Rs.75 lakhs whichever is less. The 
scheme is implemented by the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium (SFAC), an 
autonomous organization under this Ministry. Venture capital assistance is 
provided for those projects that encourage the farmers to diversify into high value crops 
and provide them with assured market and increased farm income. 
The Central Sector schemes for "Development/Strengthening of Agricultural 
Marketing Infrastructure, Grading and Standardization" and "Agribi isiness Development 
through Venture Capital Assistance" have been approved for implementation with effect from 
20.10.2004 and 11.7.2005 respectively. Assistance provided under both the schemes 
lowers the business risk to the agri-entrepreneurs and enhances the financial viability of the 
projects for the banks. Assistance is provided for the development of infrastructure projects in 
agriculture and allied sectors, and for creating user facilities like market yards, weighing 
etc., functional infrastructure like assembling, grading, labeling etc., and 
infrastructure for direct marketing, e-trading etc.

Shortage of Onion 
†*49.  DR. PRABHA THAKUR: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it iS a fact that there was acute shortage of onion in the month of 
October in the country which necessitated import of onion; 
(b) the names of the countries where from Government imported onion 
alongwith the value of onion imported, country-wise; and 
(c) the reasons for the shortage of  onion and the reasons for not 
overcoming the situation in time? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (c) 
Although the total estimated production of onion in the country in 2005 is 
59.42 lakh metric tonnes which is 4% more than the production in the previous 
year, arrival in the major wholesale markets in the country in October, 2005 was 
about 10% less than in October, 2004. This was due to erratic and excessive 
rainfall particularly in major onion growing States of Maharashtra and Gujarat 
which adversely affected the kharif onion crop significantly in those States. The 
overall kharif production has been less by 6.8% in the country as compared to 
previous year although the area under kharif is more by 3.9% than the previous 
year. The kharif crop was also delayed in some States because of the erratic 
rainfall pattern. The Government decided to import onion in view of the sudden 
spurt in prices in 3rd week of October. No import was, however, made by the 
Government as the prices soon stabilized and the market arrivals improved.

Bird flu 
*53.  SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: 
SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that World Health Organisation has warned of 
spready of Bird Flu in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have taken measures to check spreading of Bird 
Flu in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) World Health Organization (WHO) has issued an alert 
that Bird Flu could spread to India and other countries from the very first time 
that the current outbreak of Avian Influenza Virus (H5NI) was first detected in the 
Republic of Korea in December, 2003. 
Subsequently, cases in poultry and birds were reported in eleven other 
countries namely: China, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, 
Malaysia, Russia, Kazakhstan and Mongolia. 130 Human cases with 67 
deaths were reported from five countries namely: Cambodia, I ndonesia, 
Thailand, Vietnam and China (As on 17.11.2005) 
No case of Bird Flu (Avian Influenza) has been reported in India either in 
humans or birds. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry of 
Avian Influenza into India and to contain the disease if it has to happen in poultry 
or humans. The measures instituted are: 
• A joint Monitoring Group under the Chairmanship of Director 
General of Health Services consisting members from Indian Council 
of Medical Research, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, 
World Health Organization and Department of Animal Husbandry is 
monitoring the situation ever si nce the WHO alerted the global 
community and advising appropriate actions to the Government. 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
• The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying and Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of 
suspicion of outbreak of the disease and also in the event of 
outbreak of highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). A 
conference of the State Secretarie s of Animal Husbandry was held 
regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of the disease 
• Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence. Samples so far tested at High Security Animal 
Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal, were found negative. 
Training has been imparted to the staff of the State Wildlife and the 
Animal Husbandry Department, how  to collect and dispatch the 
samples to the laboratory for testing 
• There is a total ban in place against import of poultry and poultry 
related products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak 
Even birds (grand parent stock of poultry etc,) imported from highly 
pathogenic avian influenza free countries, are subjected to 
quarantine and screening. 
• Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to 
all their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory 
birds in identified water bodies Any unusual death among migratory 
birds would immediately be brought to the notice of Department of 
Animal Husbandry. 
• Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic 
Preparedness was held on 1st August, 2005, with all stakeholders to 
finalize pandemic preparedness and Response Plan. 
• A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza 
has been finalized detailing immediately action to be taken to deal 
with any suspected outbreak. The state level action plan will be 
discussed with the State Governments shortly 
• The components of the action plan such as hospital strengthening, 
Influenza Surveillance Network, Laboratory strengthening in terms 
of bio-safety labs, personal protective equipments, stockpiling of 
16 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
drugs and Information Education Communication are being taken up in a 
phased manner. 
• An Inter Ministerial Task Force has been constituted under 
Chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, 
vaccines and all other aspects for management of Avian Influenza in the 
country. 
• National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as the 
nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for investigating 
outbreaks. Under the aegis of ICMR, an Human Influenza 
surveillance network has been operationalized. 
• The situation has also been reviewed by Committee of Secretaries (on a 
monthly basis) and Ministry of Home Affairs.

into ways to make drugs available at reasonable prices; 
19

(c) whether it has already submitted its recommendations to his Ministry; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and how many of the recommendations have 
been accepted; and 
(e) the steps being taken to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (e) As per present price control policy, the 74 bulk 
drugs specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are under price control. Their 
prices are fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) 
in accordance with the provisions of the DPCO, 95. There has been no instance 
in the notice of this Department, where the entry of the new drugs is being 
blocked by present price control policy. 
A Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal 
Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options other than 
price control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable prices. The Task 
Force has submitted its report to the Government on the 20th September, 2005. 
Some of the salient recommendations of Task Force are, that Price Controls 
should be imposed on the 'essentiality' of the drug and not on the basis of 
turnover and it should be applied only to formulations and not to bulk drugs. 
Some of the other major recommendations of Task Force are to promote 
generic drugs, to encourage public health facilities, to revive the Public Sector 
Enterprises in the manufacture of drugs, to provide fiscal incentives in R&D 
activities in drugs, to provide financial support for implementation of Schedule M 
of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, to enact Drugs and Therapeutics (Regulation) Act, 
to establish a National Authority on Drugs and Therapeutics (NADT), to 
establish price negotiation process for new patented drugs, to streamline the 
bulk procurement regime, to exempt the excise duty, customs duty and other 
levies on cancer and anti HIV/AIDS drugs, to establish the State Illness Funds 
in the States/Union Territories for BPL families, to reduce the excise duty on 
drugs from 16 to 8%, to enhance the exemption limit of SSI units from Rs. 1 
crore to Rs. 5 crores, to estab lish a Settlement Commission which is 
authorized to settle the disputed overcharged amount from the pharma 
companies.

Subsidy to agriculture sector 
310. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether developed countries provide adequate subsidy to agriculture sector 
in their countries compared to India and other developing countries; 
(b) whether any proposal has been mooted to provide comparable subsidy to 
agriculture sector with a view to making it globally competitive; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) Most of 
the developed countries provide very high levels of support (both domestic and on 
exports) to their agriculture sector which distort trade in agricultural commodities 
and to a large extent make agricultural products from developing countries 
uncompetitive in the international market. For instance, as per the latest 
notifications submitted by the USA and the EC to the World Trade 
Organization (WTO), the amount of domestic support provided by them was 
around US$ 72 billion and US$ 76 billion respectively as compared to support 
level of around US$ 9 billion by India and around US$ 3 billion by Brazil. 
(b) to (d) No such proposal has been mooted. However, to make the 
agriculture globally competitive in the developing countries, including India, the 
following steps have been taken for the purpose of WTO negotiations: 
(i) India alongwith like-minded/developing countires has sought 
elimination of all forms of export subsidies by a credible end-date, and 
substantial reduction in all forms of trade distorting support provided 
by the developed countries to thei r agriculture sector. In order to 
harmonize the levels of trade-distorting domestic support permitted to be 
extended to their agriculture sector by various Members, substantial 
reductions in such domestic support will be achieved through a tiered 
formula under which Members with higher levels of domestic support 
will reduce their support by a larger amount than those with a lower 
level of support. 
57

(ii) The G-20, of which India is a Member, has also demanded that 
developing countries that allocate almost all de minimis support to 
subsistence and resource poor farmers should not be required to reduce the same

Statemen-II 
Measures taken for Tiger Conservation by Government of India 
1. Ongoing Funding Schemes: 
Funding and technical help are provided to States under the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes of "Project Tiger", "Assistance to National Parks 
& Sanctuaries" and "Project Elephant" for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastrcture of States to provide effective protection-to wild animals 
including tiger. 
2. Legal Measures Taken: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which has been amended and made 
more stringent. 
(ii) The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under 
the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and 
prosecute wildlife offenders. 
3. Administrative and other Measures: 
(i) A National Wildlife Action Plan (2002-16) has been adopted by the 
Indian Board for Wildlife under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister 
in January 2002, which outlines the strategy for conservation and 
protection of wildlife in the country. 
(ii) Government of India has set-up regional and subregional offices for 
wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country 
to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
4. International Conventions: 
India is signatory to many international conventions relating to 
biodiversity conservation and control of illegal trade in wild flora and 
fauna. 
5. Bilateral Agreements: 
India has bilateral agreements with Nepal and China for controlling trans-
boundary illegal trade in wildlife. 
90 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
6. Global tiger Forum: 
A Global tiger Forum of tiger range countries has been created for 
addressing international issues relating to tiger conservation. 
7. Initiatives Taken for eliciting public support: 
Complementary inputs for Ecodevelopment and voluntary village 
relocation provided earlier in separate projects have now been merged 
with Project Tiger as an "Umbrella Scheme". 
Under the externally aided "India Eco-development Project", as many 
as 572 eco-development committees  have been formed in seven 
Projected Areas (which included six Tiger Reserves) covering 75,600 
families, to reduce the dependency of local people on Protected Area 
resources, with reciprocal commitments. An amount of Rs. 15,692.30 
lakhs has been provided to States for 6 Tiger Reserves till the 
completion of this Project in 2004. 
8. Other Initiatives Taken: 
— Eight more potential sites have been identified for Project Tiger 
coverage. 
— "Project Allowance" has been provided under the scheme to field staff 
working in tiger reserves. 
— Regional Monitoring of Tiger Reserves has been done by a group of 
experts as per the normative standards of the Ministry. 
— 100% Central Assistance is provided for deploying anti-poaching strike 
squads in Tiger Reserves, apart from expenditure relating to research, 
veterinary, monitoring and evaluation, compensation to the legal heir of 
staff/person killed while performing duty, and for monitoring of tiger 
population. 
— Information and communication technology is under use for linking 
important tiger reserves in the GIS Domain for evolving a 
management support system and crime detection, dissemination of 
information through web and evolving a 'National Tiger Monitoring and 
Habitat Evaluation System' with regional protocols. 
— The allocation under Project Tige r has been enhanced from Rs. 
7500 lakhs in the IX Plan to Rs. 15,000 lakhs in the X Plan.

state: 
(a) the details of the rules and regulations governing prevention of food 
adulteration in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the existing laws have proved to be ineffective in 
preventing food adulteration in the country; 
(c) whether any comparative study has been undertaken between the Indian 
laws and those adopted by the Developed Nations to learn how those countries 
have succeeded in nearly eliminating food adulteration and the shortcomings 
of the Indian laws; and 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, whether such a study would be 
instituted? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) Adulteration in 
food stuffs is checked and regulated in the country under the provisions of 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rules, 1955. The Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Act has been amended thrice so far, in 1964, 1976 and 1986 to plug 
the loop-holes and make the law more stringent and also to empower the 
recognized consumer organizations to play active role in the Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Programme. 
The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the rules made thereunder 
provide for adequate provisions to check and curb the adulteration and 
misbranding of food articles. The Act provides for strict penal provisions against 
the offenders. 
Standards of quality have been laid down under the Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Rules, 1955 for more than 270 articles of food. Most of the rules 
and regulations laid down under these rules are in conformity with the 
guidelines laid down by the Codex Alimentarious Commission, an 
International body of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and 
World Health Organisation (WHO) of the United Nations.

WHO report on health 
369. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent report of the World Health 
Organisation titled "Preventing global diseases a vital investment" highlighting 
inter-alia that over the next 10 years, 388 million people will die from non-
communicable diseases such as heart diseases, cancer and diabetes with 
economic consequences for various countries, including India which would suffer 
to the extent of some $ 236 billion; 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
(b) if so, the results thereof; and 
(c) the details of other major findings/observations contained in the report 
and the fresh steps initiated for prevention of such diseases and avoidable high 
death rate? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a)to (c) WHO'S Report 
titled "Preventing Chronic Diseases -AVital Investment" has been globally 
launched recently. The report points out that 80% of chronic disease deaths occur in 
low and middle-income countries including India. The problem of chronic 
diseases (i.e. heart disease, stroke, di abetes, injuries etc.) has major adverse 
effects on the quality of life of affected individuals, causes premature death and 
creates large adverse and underapprec iated economic effects on families, 
communities and societies in general. The low and middle income countries are 
expected to forego a substantial part of their national income over the next 10 
years as result of premature deaths caused by heart disease, stroke and 
diabetes. 
The report has called upon the World community to implement 
comprehensive and integrated approaches that encompass interventions directed 
at both the whole populations and individuals focusing on the common 
underlying risk factors cutting across specific diseases. 
The Government of India is already implementing various public health 
programmes both at policy level and grass root levels, laying stress on research 
and training of medical personnel in the field of chronic diseases. 
Besides specific programmes the National Rural Health Mission launched 
recently also seeks to promote a hea lthy lifestyle for prevention of chronic 
diseases. 
Some of the specific steps initiated in this regard are listed below: 
* The Indian Council of Medical  Research and World Health 
Organisation have undertaken studies on Non-Communicable 
Disease (NCD) risk factor prevalence in five centers in India and based 
on this model, the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme 
(IDSP) has incorporated NCD risk factor surveillance as a programme 
component. 
* The National Cancer Control Programme has been revised recently to 
make it more effective. 
* Standard treatment guidelines fo r Diabetes, Asthama and Chronic 
Obstructive Lung Diseases have been developed. 
128 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* Tobacco, the single most important risk factor for chronic diseases, has 
been addressed in India through a comprehensive legislation and various 
other interventions. 
* Health promotion and advocacy efforts have been taken up along with 
Integrated NCD prevention programmes in various parts of India with 
focus on industrial populations. 
* The Ministrty of Health and Family Welfare in collaboration with the 
WHO has initiated follow up action on the WHO Global Strategy on Diet, 
Physical Activity and Health which offers various avenues to increase 
vegetable and fruit consumption and increase physical activity.

SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) No case of Bird 
Flu (Avian Influenza) has been reported in India either in humans or birds. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry of 
Avian Influenza in to India and to cont ain the disease if it has to happen in 
poultry or humans. The measures instituted are: 
• A Joint Monitoring Group under the Chairmanship of Director 
General of Health Services constituting members from Indian 
Council of Medical Research, National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases, World Health Organizat ion and Department of Animal 
Husbandry is monitoring the situation ever since the WHO alerted the 
global community and advising appropriate actions to the 
Government. 
• The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying and Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
134 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of 
suspicion of outbreak of the disease and also in the event of 
outbreak of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). A 
conference of the State Secretarie s of Animal Husbandry was held 
regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of the disease. 
• Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence. Samples so far tested at High Security Animal Disease 
Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal were found negative. Training has been 
imparted to the staff of the State Wildlife and the Animal Husbandry 
Department, how to collect and dispatch the samples to the laboratory 
for testing. 
• There is a total ban in place against import of poultry and poultry 
related products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak. (Even 
birds [grant parent stock of poultry etc.) imported from highly pathogenic 
avian influenza free countries ar e subjected to quarantine and 
screening. 
• Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to all 
their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory birds in 
identified water bodies. Any unusual death among migratory birds would 
immediately be brought to the notice of Department of Animal 
Husbandry. 
• Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation. A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic 
Preparedness was held on 1 "August,  2005 with all stakeholders to 
finalize pandemic preparedness and Response Plan. 
• A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza has 
been finalized detailing immediate action to be taken to deal with any 
suspected outbreak. The State level action plan will be discussed with 
the State Governments, shortly. 
• The com ponents of the action plan such as hospitals strengthening, 
Influenza Surveillance Network, laboratory strengthening in terms of bio-
safety labs, personal protective equipments, stockpiling of drugs and 
Information Education Communication are being taken up in a phased 
manner. 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
• An Inter Ministerial Task Force has been constituted under the 
chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, 
vaccines and all other aspects for management of Avian Influenza in the 
country. 
• National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as the 
nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for investigating 
outbreaks. Under the aegis of ICMR, an Human Influenza 
surveillance network has been operationalised. 
• The situation has also been reviewed by Committee of Secretaries and 
Ministry of Home Affairs. 
Because of the proactive steps taken by the Government, there is no spread 
of Avian Influenza from neighbouring countries in to India.

Iodised salt and goitre 
 †376. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the methodology to prove that non-iodised salt plays a vital role in 
causing goitre and mental retardation in children in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have no means to prevent the 
diseases caused due to consumption of excess quantity of iodine by. using 
iodised salt; 
(c) if so, the rationale behind making the sale of iodised salts compulsory; and 
(d) the reasons for Government's intention for initiating an international 
debate on the issue instead of doing it at the national level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) It is well 
established medical fact that nutritional iodine deficiency results in a 
spectrum of diseases designated as Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) which 
include goitre, mental and physical retardation, still birth, neuromotor defects, 
cretins etc. Most of the Iodine deficiency disorders are permanent and incurable 
in nature except a few types of goitre, but all these can be prevented by regular 
consumption of iodised salt. 
In our country, the iodine level in salt at the consumption level is 15 ppm 
(parts per million) while at production level it is 30 ppm. The average 
consumption of iodised salt per person per day is 10 gm. Thus the 
possibility of excess consumption of iodine through iodised salt does not arise. 
The iodine level of iodised salt is absolutely safe. In Japan, the consumption 
of iodine is upto 3000 microgram per day and they have not 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
139 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
noticed any ill effects including iodine induced hyperthyroidism. Further the 
excess of iodine in the body is excreted in urine which is measured as urinary 
iodine excretion. 
About 92 countries are implementing compulsory iodisation of salt. 
Iodised salt is the most effective and cost effective way to prevent and control 
this problem. This has been well documented by WHO and UNICEF. The iodine 
deficiency disorders are prevalent in the entire country and no State/UT is free 
from goitre and other IDD. These were the reasons that led to the Governments 
took decision to ban the sale of non-iodised salt for direct human consumption 
as a public health measure.

WHO'S report on killer diseases 
399. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Health Organization has in its recent report given a 
wake-up call to India to squarely meet the challenges of some killer diseases 
in the country. 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to meet the challenges highlighted 
in the WHO Report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMl): (a) and (b) The World 
Health Organization in its various reports in 2005 has identified the emergence 
of pandermics of SARS, Avian influenza, dengue fever, Japanese encephalitis, 
Leptosphirosis and drug resistant malaria which slowly but steadily have 
entrenched themselves in the large parts of South East Asia 
160 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Region including India. WHO has also pointed out that the recent occurrence of Avian 
influenza in various Asian countries demands greater attention by the national 
authorities to immediately strengt hen the recognitio n and response 
mechanisms, infrastructure and expertise. The WHO has also warned that these 
emerging diseases will continue to challenge public health systems for many 
years to come. A well developed strategy and programme shall have to be 
implemented through a coordinated and pragmatic plan and a vigilant public 
health system for effective containment of these diseases. 
(c) The Government has an elaborate network in place to contain diseases 
like SARS, Avian Influenza, Dengue, Japanese Encephalitis, Leprospirosis and 
drug resistant malaria. Institutions like National Institute of Communicable 
Disease (NICD) are constantly engaged in research and investigation to check 
outbreak and to control the diseases. 
The National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme (NVBDCP) is 
functional in all States to meet the challenge of Malaria, Dengue Fever and 
Japanese Encephalitis. 
To prevent spread of Avian Influenza to India, periodic reviews have been 
regularly conducted since 2003. There is an Avian Influenza Monitoring Cell in 
NICD, which has been designated the nodal agency for implementing contingency 
plan which includes forming Rapid Response Teams and stockpiling of 
Chemo prophylaxis drugs. 
For creating and sustaining strong and vigilant public health system, the 
integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP) has been launched in November, 2004. 
IDSP is designed not only for surveillance and response for the diseases labeled by 
WHO as killer Diseases but also to meet the challenges of unknown diseases in future. 
A substantial part of the country has already been covered by IDSP which will 
extend to the whole country by 2006.    .

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. Gas Authority 
of India Limited (GAIL) is working with M/s Sumitomo Chemical Co. Ltd., 
Japan for development of facilities for manufacturing of long lasting 
insecticide (Pyrethroid) impregnate d HDPE polymer nets (LLIN). The

on sample of polymer supplied by the party. 
(b) There are 3 major groups of insecticides being used by the National Vector 
Borne Disease Control Programme for control of Malaria through Indoor 
Residual Spraying (IRS): 
1.  Chlorinated Hydrocarbon Group: DDT 50% WDP (Water Dispersible 
Powder) 
Indoor Residual Spraying with DDT 50% WDP had been quite effective in the 
prevention of malaria menace. IRS with DDT remains effective for a period of 2 to 
3 months and hence 2 round of IRS are carried out in different States depending upon 
the period of malaria transmission season. However, in the areas where the malaria 
vectors have developed resistance to DDT, it has been replaced with other group 
of insecticides. 
2. Organophosphorous Group: Malathion 25% WDP 
Indoor Residual Spraying with Malathion 25% WDP had been quite 
effective in the prevention of malari a menace. IRS with Malathion remains 
effective for a period of 1 to 2 months and hence 3 rounds of IRS are carried 
in different States depending upon the pe riod of malaria transmission season. 
However, in the areas where the malaria vectors have developed resistance to 
Malathion, it is replaced with other group of insecticides. 
3. Synthetic Pyrethroid Group: This is a new group of insecticides. 
There are many compounds in this group of insecticides. However, the 
following insecticides of this group are being used in malaria control 
programme: 
i) Deltamethrin 2.5% 
ii) Cyfluthrin 10%

iii) Lambdacyhalothrin 10% 
iv) Alphacypermethrin 5%

Pyrethroids remains effective for a period of 2 to 3 months and hence 2 rounds of IRS are 
carried to cover States depending upon the period of malaria transmission season. In areas 
where the malaria vectors have developed resistance to DDT and Malathion, Synthetic 
Pyrethroids group of insecticides are recommended.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) There is no categorization of Railway bridges as outdated. Railway 
undertakes repair, rehabilitation/rebuilding of bridges on the basis of their physical 
condition as ascertained during annual inspections and not on the basis of age. 
Few bridges which may show signs of deterioration of physical condition 
indicating need for rehabilitation on priority are classified as Distressed 
Bridges. Depending upon nature of defect and classification the 
repair/rebuilding/rehabilitation of such bridges is taken up on priority. 
Total No. of bridges rehabilitated/rebuilt during last five years is 
approximately 5667. Such statistics are not maintained, State-wise. 
(b) and (c) Mobile phones have not been provided to gangmen and there is no 
such plan. However, on some zonal Railways Walkie-Talkie sets are provided to 
patrolmen patrolling the railway track during emergency. 
(d) The following steps have been taken, for improving safety on Indian 
Railway as far as track is concerned. 
(i) Regular inspection of track at various levels is undertaken. 
(ii) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of track 
sophisticated recording cars and oscillograph cars are being used. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005]

recruitment and thereafter their knowledge is refreshed periodically. 
Seminars/workshops/field demonstrations are also organized for 
Permanent Way staff from time to time to enhance/update their 
knowledge. 
(iv) Patrolling of Railway track by gangmen is carried out at vulnerable 
locations during monsoon, summer and winter. 
(v) The specifications of rail steel have been upgraded and are in 
conformity with the International Union of Railways (UIC) 
specifications. 
(vi) Ultrasonic Flaw Detectors are used to detect hidden flaws in the rail. 
(vii) Mechanized maintenance of track is being introduced progressively, 
for better and improved maintenance. 
(viii) The track structure is being upgraded on a planned basis. 
(ix) To keep the track in good cond ition, track renewals are carried out 
whenever it becomes due for renewal subject to availability of funds.

424. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that present rail engines are more powerful than the 
earlier coal/steam engines;

186 

[25 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA

to bear the forceful speed of the ra il engines today and as a result thereof 
accidents are increasing; and

capacity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R.VELU):(a)Yes, Sir.

the years, track structure has been upgraded with rails of larger cross section,

only if the track structure is adequate for the purpose.

Khanna Rail Accident Report 
  428. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:          
SHRI HARISH RAWAT:   
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Khanna railway accident report has been submitted and if 
so, the details thereof; and 
(b) the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (b) Justice G. C. Garg Commission in his report 
submitted on 16.7.2004 has concluded that, the rail accident near Khanna occurred 
on account of a gap created in the continuity of the long welded right rail of the 
up track on 26.11.1998. Rear right trolley of coach No. 10 of the Up train derailed 
in the first instance and coaches following that coach continued to derail and 
started moving in an unguided manner for some distance. One or more than one 
derailed coaches in that process also capsized and infringed the adjoining down 
track. Transverse fatigue cracks are the cause of rail failure. The initiation of 
flaws, which assumed the shape of transverse fatigue cracks, was because of 
excessive non-metallic inclusions. As a result of detrailment of the coaches of 
the Up train, the down track was infringed and the down train hit the 
derailed/capsized coaches of the Up trai n. The cause as established by the 
Commission has been accepted by the Government. 
Directorate of Track Procurement of Railway Board, Northern Railway, 
Director General of Supplies & Disposal and Bhilai Steel Plant of Steel 
Authority of India Limited have been  held equally responsible. Primary 
responsibility of engine crew of Up train has also been accepted. 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2005] 
In this report total 44 recommendations were made out of which 23 have 
been accepted, 17 were partially accepted and 4 have not been found feasible 
for acceptance. 
The report with Action Taken by the Government thereon was laid in the Rajya

(a) whether Government are aware that during last three years, several senior

(SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Three senior officers (Junior

Western Railway and Diesel Loco Modernisation Works, were accused of sexual 
harassment. As the Railways are organized Zone-wise, State-wise information is

option to seek transfer of the accused officer or of their own transfer.
